title: Cost Optimization: Dimensionality Reduction and Quantization

questions.q: Per the chapter's storage table, how much space do 10 million 1536-dimensional vectors (text-embedding-3-small) need as float32, int8, and binary respectively?
questions.explain: The chapter's table shows 1536-dim text-embedding-3-small at 10M vectors: 58 GB float32, 14.6 GB int8, and 1.8 GB binary - binary being the 1-bit-per-dimension endgame of quantization.

questions.q: Why is Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) advantageous for dimensionality reduction compared to PCA?
options: MRL-trained models (e.g. text-embedding-3-small/large) are trained so the first N dimensions are themselves a valid, high-quality embedding - you truncate natively via the API's dimensions parameter with no projection matrix and no query-time transformation
MRL requires fitting a projection matrix on 100k sample vectors
MRL only works with int8 quantized vectors
MRL increases dimensions instead of reducing them
questions.explain: With MRL you truncate rather than project: no projection matrix to store, no transformation at query time, and better quality than PCA because the model was explicitly trained for reduced dimensions. OpenAI supports native truncation via the dimensions parameter.

questions.q: What runtime cost does PCA-based dimensionality reduction impose that MRL truncation avoids?
options: The embedding API must be called twice per query
PCA vectors cannot use cosine similarity
The projection matrix must be stored and applied to every new query vector at search time (with L2 normalization required after projection for cosine search)
PCA requires rebuilding the entire database on each query
questions.explain: The chapter notes the projection matrix must be stored and applied to every new query vector at search time - this is PCA's runtime cost - and vectors must be L2-normalized after projection when using cosine similarity.

questions.q: How much memory does scalar quantization to int8 save per dimension, and how is recall preserved in Qdrant's production pattern?
options: 2x savings; recall is preserved by doubling dimensions
8x savings; recall is preserved by re-embedding on the fly

4x savings (4 bytes to 1 byte per dimension), with near-full recall via quantization with rescoring: quantized vectors select candidates in RAM, top candidates are re-scored with original float32 vectors
32x savings with no recall impact at all
questions.explain: Scalar quantization maps float32 to int8 - 4 bytes to 1 byte, a 4x reduction. Qdrant's production pattern is 'quantization with rescoring': fast candidate selection on quantized vectors, then re-score top candidates (oversampling ~2.0) with original float32 vectors for near-full recall.

questions.q: What compression levers does the chapter identify for SQL Server 2025's native VECTOR type?
options: Built-in float16 and binary-quantized column types

The VECTOR type is float32 only with no built-in float16 or binary-quantized column type - levers are storing fewer dimensions via MRL truncation, quantizing at the application layer before insert, and the two-phase pattern (compact candidates, exact rescore)
Automatic compression via row/page compression on VECTOR columns
The engine transparently quantizes to int8 during DiskANN builds
questions.explain: The chapter states the native VECTOR type stores float32 with no built-in float16 or binary-quantized type. Levers are MRL truncation to fewer dimensions, application-layer quantization before insert, and the two-phase pattern: compact 512-dim candidates then rescore with full float32 vectors.
